clue.text: One who went at 15mph at start of seaside rails

blocks.note: Roger Bannister ran the first four-minute mile in 1954, averaging about 15mph
first letter of seaside

explanation.surface: Someone speeding along the railings at the start of a seaside promenade.
explanation.walkthrough: A four-minute mile works out at 15 miles an hour, which is the only clue to the runner. Banisters are the rails of a staircase; this spelling with two Ns is an accepted variant.
explanation.definitionFit: Bannisters are the handrails running up a staircase.

clue.text: Clobber boy in front of tree

blocks.note: B is a dictionary abbreviation for boy
the ash is a tree

explanation.surface: An instruction to beat up a lad standing in front of a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Clobber is a verb here, to hit, not the British slang noun for clothes or gear.
explanation.definitionFit: To bash someone is to clobber them, to hit them hard.

clue.text: In reflection of river, a bright star

blocks.note: the Avon is an English river, the one at Stratford

explanation.surface: A bright star seen mirrored in the surface of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine picture of a star shining on water, which is exactly the reflection that turns AVON round.
explanation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares to many times its usual brightness.

clue.text: ... regardless of price (it veers wildly)

indicators.note: the letters are thrown about at random

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: Buying something whatever it costs, as prices swing about.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots link this to the clue before, a setter's flourish that doesn't change the parse. The brackets are only surface punctuation; the fodder runs straight through them.
explanation.definitionFit: Irrespective of means regardless of, taking no account of.

clue.text: Characteristic of balding Cockney – where it's all vanished!

indicators.note: a Cockney accent drops the H at the start of words

blocks.note: a balding man has thin hair
the H of HAIR is dropped, as a Cockney says 'air

explanation.surface: A Cockney who is going bald, and whose hair has all disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class London accent, famous for dropping H. Things that vanish into thin air disappear without trace, which is where the balding man's hair has gone too.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that disappears completely is said to vanish into thin air.

clue.text: Enters the price of phones

blocks.note: what a shop assistant does at the till
to ring someone up is British for phoning them

explanation.surface: Looking up what phones cost.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'the price of phones' as one phrase; split it after 'price' and each half is a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringing up a sale records its price on the till; ringing someone up telephones them.

clue.text: Steals judge's clothes, wanting piece of ermine

blocks.note: judges wear robes
first letter of ermine, removed from ROBES

explanation.surface: A thief pinching a judge's robes, though without the ermine trim.
explanation.walkthrough: Ermine, the white fur trim on ceremonial robes, keeps the surface in the courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to rob is to steal from someone, as the thief in the surface does to the judge.

clue.text: In a gaudy way, like a gilet might be sported?

definitions.text: like a gilet might be sported?

blocks.note: excessively, flashily

blocks.clueFragment: like a gilet might be sported?
blocks.note: a gilet is a sleeveless jacket, worn on top of a shirt or jumper

explanation.surface: A question about whether a gilet is a showy piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is taken literally: a gilet, a sleeveless padded jacket, is worn over your top. The question mark flags that playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Over the top means excessive or flamboyant, as a gaudy outfit is.

clue.text: Emphasize international investigation of pressure

blocks.note: to stress a point is to emphasize it
a Test is an international cricket or rugby match

explanation.surface: Stressing the importance of an international inquiry into pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: International reads as an adjective but stands for a noun: a Test match, the international fixture in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A stress test checks how a system, or a bank, copes under pressure.

clue.text: Gold coins ... heads!

blocks.note: the sovereign is a British gold coin
heads of state, monarchs

explanation.surface: Tossing gold coins and calling heads.
explanation.walkthrough: Heads suggests the side of a coin, and the monarch's head is on it, but here it means rulers themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Sovereigns are both British gold coins and the monarchs who head a state.

clue.text: Look, Lord

blocks.note: a verb: to look closely or searchingly
a member of the House of Lords

explanation.surface: An exclamation: Look, Lord!
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes it read as someone calling a lord's attention; each word is its own definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Peer means both to look searchingly and a member of the nobility.

clue.text: Never file and cut recklessly (without thought)

definitions.note: an adjective phrase, as the answer is

indicators.note: the letters are thrown together carelessly

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Advice to a careless manicurist: don't file, just hack away.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'and' simply glues the two lots of fodder together.
explanation.definitionFit: An unreflective person acts without thinking things over.

clue.text: Dispatches pair of idiots in a trial that ends abruptly

indicators.note: the word is cut off before its last letter

blocks.note: two asses
used as it stands
used as it stands
TEST without its last T

explanation.surface: A news report of two fools being sent off in a trial cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: Dispatches looks like a noun, news reports, but is a verb meaning kills. 'In a' reads as linking words and is wordplay taken straight.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispatch someone is to kill them, as an assassin does.

clue.text: Ungodliest changes that are seen all round the world

definitions.text: that are seen all round the world
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the things themselves

indicators.note: the letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: The most wicked changes, spreading worldwide.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose and cryptic: lines of longitude run right round the globe from pole to pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines of longitude encircle the earth through both poles.

clue.text: Reckless exec, Samuel, offering implausible justification

indicators.note: the letters are treated carelessly, jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A rash executive called Samuel trying to explain himself away.
explanation.walkthrough: Reckless reads as a description of Samuel, but it is an instruction to scramble the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: lame means feeble, so a feeble reason offered to excuse yourself is one nobody believes.

clue.text: Carousing, drunk aeronaut stripped of uniform

blocks.note: a balloonist or airman
U is Uniform in the NATO alphabet; it is removed

explanation.surface: A drunken airman on a spree, out of uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the U out of AERONAUT, then rearrange what is left. Uniform suggests clothes but is just the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: On a tear is informal for on a drinking spree, carousing.

clue.text: Here's a gift

blocks.note: the answer at a roll call
something given, a noun

explanation.surface: Someone handing over a gift: here you are.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is', joining two definitions that mean the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Present means both here, in attendance, and a gift.

clue.text: Larger kitchen implement, did you say?

indicators.note: asks whether you heard it right, so go by sound

blocks.note: a grater shreds cheese

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone wanted a bigger kitchen gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: Larger could describe the implement, but it is the definition; the kitchen tool only supplies the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: greater and larger are both comparatives meaning of bigger size.

clue.text: Listing about ... one noisy reveller

indicators.note: the list goes round the other piece

blocks.note: a roster is a list of duties
I = one, placed inside RO-STER

explanation.surface: Something listing, then one rowdy partygoer.
explanation.walkthrough: Listing suggests leaning over, as a drunk might, but it is the noun, a list. Roister is usually a verb; as a noun, meaning a roisterer, it is rare.
explanation.definitionFit: A roister is an old word for a roisterer, a noisy reveller.

clue.text: German acknowledges grim sort of humour

definitions.note: the answer is the noun used as a modifier, as in gallows humour

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German
to allow a point is to acknowledge it

explanation.surface: A German admits to having a dark sense of humour.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition names the phrase the answer completes: gallows humour is jokes made in grim circumstances.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallows humour is dark humour about death or disaster.

clue.text: Some scallywag ran a dairy somewhere in Spain

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: hidden in scallywaG RAN A DAiry

explanation.surface: A rogue running a dairy farm in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is set in Spain already, so it is easy to hunt for a place name elsewhere rather than inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Granada is a city in Andalusia, southern Spain.

clue.text: Shirking one's duties?

blocks.note: dodging, getting out of paying
duties read as obligations, but a duty is also a tax, as in customs duty

explanation.surface: Someone dodging their responsibilities.
explanation.walkthrough: Duties reads as obligations, but duties are also taxes on goods, so shirking them is avoiding tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Tax avoidance is legally arranging your affairs to pay less tax.

clue.text: Second-hand, unsteady, regularly failing

blocks.note: U n S t E a D y, keeping the odd letters

explanation.surface: An old, wobbly machine that breaks down again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Regularly failing sounds like a description of a clapped-out car, but it tells you to lose every second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Used means second-hand, previously owned.

clue.text: Somewhat saucy and kind of blue

indicators.note: only part of the words is taken

blocks.note: hidden in sauCY ANd

explanation.surface: Something a bit cheeky and slightly risqué, a blue joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue here also plays on its sense of rude, which suits saucy, but the definition is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: cyan is one particular shade, the greenish blue of printer ink.

clue.text: Grimly obstinate, Everyman's after last bit of custard

blocks.note: last letter of custard
Everyman is everybody, so what is Everyman's is ours: OUR

explanation.surface: The setter sulkily determined to get the last of the custard.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name, usually for ME or MY; Everyman is everyone, so it gives OUR here.
explanation.definitionFit: Dour means stern and obstinately gloomy.

clue.text: Composer, pious type, yellin' – by heavens!

blocks.note: a saint, abbreviated ST
ravin' = raving, yelling; the dropped G matches
the heavens are the sky

explanation.surface: A devout type shouting out a composer's name as an oath.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in yellin' tells you the G is dropped, so RAVIN' not RAVING. 'By heavens!' reads as an oath but just joins SKY on.
explanation.definitionFit: Igor Stravinsky was the Russian composer of The Rite of Spring.

clue.text: Writing may be done on this feature, with beginning and end discarded

definitions.text: Writing may be done on this

indicators.note: the first and last letters are dropped

blocks.note: an aspect is a feature
ASPECT loses A and T

explanation.surface: A feature of paper that makes it good for writing on, trimmed at both ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Writing on spec means writing speculatively, without a commission, so 'on this' is the phrase on spec.
explanation.definitionFit: Freelancers write on spec, hoping to sell the piece afterwards.

clue.text: As Revelation mentions, apocalyptic gathering engendering devastating destruction of Nature, primarily?

definitions.text: As Revelation mentions, apocalyptic gathering engendering devastating destruction of Nature, primarily?

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: As Revelation mentions, apocalyptic gathering engendering devastating destruction of Nature
blocks.note: the first letter of each of these ten words

explanation.surface: A description of the final battle foretold in the Book of Revelation.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its initials spell the answer, and read straight it describes Armageddon, the gathering place of the last battle in Revelation.
explanation.definitionFit: Armageddon is the site of the final battle between good and evil in Revelation.
